transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
It's Election Day.
Polls have just opened in many states in the central U.S., including Texas.
That state is home to the most expensive Senate race in U.S. history.
The candidates made their closing arguments in San Antonio.
From Texas Public Radio Andrea Drush reports.
In deep red Texas, Democrats are the underdogs,
and James Tallarico is invoking the football drama Friday Night Lights.
Six immortal words. Clear eyes. Full hearts. Dant boots.
But in an unusual election year, most polls show a close race,
and many even have Tallarico up.
About 20 miles away, in a bar called the Angry Elephant,
Republican Ken Paxman warned conservatives that if the fractured party doesn't come together,
this seemingly impossible could happen.
Texas has never been this close in a slipping way.
More than 40 percent of Texas's registered voters cast their ballots during early voting,
breaking the state's 2018 midterm turnout record.
I'm Andrea Drush in San Antonio.
The U.S. Supreme Court has denied a last-minute request from the Trump administration
to wade into an unprecedented feud with California.
It's over that state's voter rolls.
NPR's Jude Joffe block reports the denial came just hours after the Justice Department appealed.
The Justice Department wanted the high court to force California election officials
to set aside ballots that pertain to 20,000 people that federal officials say are likely non-citizens.
But California election officials and data experts have argued the DOJ's list is full of errors.
Plus, they've said segregating ballots isn't feasible with voting already underway.
The Supreme Court's refusal to take on the case comes after both a federal judge
and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the DOJ's demand last week,
citing that the Constitution gives states authority to run elections.
Plus, federal courts tend to avoid changing voting rules right before an election.
Jude Joffe block, NPR News.
Iran has been watching the U.S. midterms closely.
Iran has used the national vote as part of a pressure campaign
to try to draw the Trump administration back to negotiations instead of to renewed conflict.
And Pierre's Hadil al-Shelchi reports officials in Arab Gulf nations
are also engaging in diplomatic efforts to try to stop any new war.
Gulf countries like Saudi Arabia and the UAE end up shouldering the brunt of Iran's retaliation
to U.S. Israeli strikes because Iran attacks U.S. bases on their land.
And feeling abandoned by the U.S., the Gulf has been hurriedly trying to take matters
into its own hands in the past few weeks by talking directly to Iran.
There's been a flurry of diplomatic visits between Tehran and mediator country Qatar.
We heard from an Emirati diplomatic adviser yesterday that the Gulf is bracing for the worst.
And then on Monday, Trump posted on his social media that an agreement with Iran "could happen."
And Pierre's Hadil al-Shelchi reporting. This is NPR.
The White House has just announced that First Lady Melania Trump
will host officials from Ukraine and Russia at the White House this week.
Trump administration officials say Mrs. Trump helped broker a recent ceasefire
in the Ukrainian town of Olshat Al-Lashki. Civilians there were allowed to evacuate.
Those who remained were given humanitarian aid.
Mrs. Trump is scheduled to speak about the ceasefire this Thursday.
Big tech company Apple is reporting strong earnings in its latest quarter.
But the company's share price got dinged.
That's because Apple is predicting it will pay higher prices for memory chips
and face tighter supply chain problems.
NPR's John Ruich reports.
Apple's revenue in the September quarter rose 12 percent year-on-year,
hitting a quarterly record and beating Wall Street's expectations.
But in recent months, the company has been forced to raise prices on several products
because the cost of memory chips has been soaring as demand from AI data centers skyrockets.
On a call with analysts, Apple executives said they expect that pressure to continue into the next quarter.
Apple's share price dropped by as much as 4.5 percent in after-hours trading before rebounding a bit.
John Ruich, NPR News.
Two people are believed to have died in Arizona after several days of flooding.
That hit the Four Corners area where Arizona touches Colorado, New Mexico and Utah.
Some areas got more rain in a day than they do in a month.
There's heavy rain reported this morning on Central Florida's Atlantic coast.
Flood watch a stretch from Daytona to past Cape Canaveral.
It's NPR.

topics.text: Polls open in central U.S. states, including Texas, on Election Day amid record Senate spending
Texas Senate race between Tallarico and Paxton is close, with record early voter turnout
Supreme Court denies Trump administration's request to force California to set aside suspected non-citizen ballots
Gulf states pursue direct diplomacy with Iran to head off renewed war with U.S. and Israel
First Lady Melania Trump to host Ukrainian and Russian officials at White House after Olshansky ceasefire
Apple reports record September-quarter revenue but warns of higher memory chip costs and supply pressure
Flooding in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah's Four Corners area kills two people
